meta.title: Decision Model Report
meta.description: Validating a 37-76 ms 0.8B /v1/systemone distillation pipeline on H100 + vLLM across OpenShift/Metal3 bare-metal root-cause analysis (94.0% synthetic, 22.9% real issues) and a controlled real-time benchmark (425 vs Jev's 178).

hero.kicker: Conclusion First · Experimental Report on 0.8B Decision Models
hero.title: Decision Model Report
hero.subtitle: First, the right scenario (closed options and strict latency). Second, clean structured data and verified labels. Third, a disciplined training regimen that prevents overfitting. Below is our conclusion upfront, followed by experimental proof from Bare-Metal RCA (`baremetal-rca`) and our real-time control benchmark (`decision-pacman`).

kpis.footprint_delta: RCA student: 94.0% on 333 synthetic cases. Validation rose from 21.8% before training to 90.2% after training.
kpis.training_label: Real tickets and a distribution gap

rca.kicker: Experimental Proof 01 · Bare-Metal Provisioning RCA (OpenShift / Metal3 / Ironic)
rca.title: Bare-metal RCA scores 94.0% on synthetic cases and 22.9% on real issues
rca.lead: Without changing a single line of training or serving code (`build_sft.py`, `train.py`, `scripts/systemone_vllm.ts`), we applied the exact same 0.8B pipeline to triage failed OpenShift bare-metal installations across 23 root-cause classes (`bmc_credentials`, `dhcp_not_reaching`, `boot_mode_mismatch`, `api_ingress_vip_dns`, `product_bug`, etc.).
rca.synth_title: The 0.8B student gets 313 of 333 synthetic cases right
rca.synth_body: Using Apache 2.0 OKD, OpenShift, and Metal3 troubleshooting documentation, a 27B model generated structured incident summaries. We used 1,128 for training and 225 for validation. LoRA training took 141 steps, about 3 minutes on one H100; validation accuracy rose from 21.8% to 90.2%. The separate synthetic evaluation contains 333 cases written by DeepSeek-V4-Flash.
rca.real_title: The historical student gets 11 of 48 real issues right
rca.real_body: Of 236 closed issues from metal3-io/baremetal-operator, metal3-io/ironic-image, and openshift/installer, 77 described failures and 48 had settled root causes. One annotator labeled 34 product bugs and 14 configuration or environment failures. The historical student got 10/34 product bugs and 1/14 other cases right; DeepSeek got 15/34 and 5/14. Differences in class balance, incomplete reports, and label ambiguity may explain the gap, but their causal contributions have not been tested.
rca.real_bar_audit: 671B MoE teacher with maintainer comments vs human RCA
rca.conditions_title: What the two tasks suggest about deployment
rca.conditions_lead: The game and RCA results motivate the checks below. The cause of the RCA synthetic-to-real gap remains untested.
rca.c1_title: Suitable Scenario: Closed Options & Fast Decisions
rca.c1_body: The decision is a legal move or one of 23 root-cause classes. The recorded 0.8B models answer these closed choices in 37–76 ms on their respective measured hardware. The 21.8% RCA figure is pretraining validation accuracy, not a Jev benchmark.
rca.c2_title: Clean Input Data: Engine Telemetry vs Human Ticket Prose
rca.c2_body: The game encoder computes distances and counts from the engine. Real issue summaries can omit fields and retain the reporter's guesses. Testing better input capture is a next step, not a verified remedy.
rca.c3_title: Clean Labels: Simulator Rollouts vs Noisy Teacher Labels
rca.c3_body: Pac-Man teacher labels use five-second rollouts. RCA real-case labels come from one annotator; a teacher reading maintainer comments agreed on only 5 of 14 configuration or environment cases. This exposes label ambiguity, but does not measure a student accuracy ceiling.
rca.c4_body: RCA training was approximately balanced, but 70.8% of real cases are product bugs. This mismatch is a possible explanation for the accuracy drop. Separately, the Pac-Man two-epoch run raised offline validation accuracy but lowered gameplay from 423 to 266 pellets.

play.lead: Games are not our business, but Pac-Man intersections satisfy all four conditions for Jev and /v1/systemone (closed choices, exact BFS facts, 5s simulator rollouts, and matched trajectories). Play the same 30-second seed to experience what the models receive.

halo.title: It is not that mysterious
halo.lead: Take an ordinary open-source model with zero decision training and constrain its output. It plays about as well as Jev.
halo.chart_note: Historical off-the-shelf models, hosted APIs, and scripted rules cluster between 148 and 237; the distilled 0.8B reaches 425. Players receive the same facts and legal choices through their respective APIs. Means aggregate different run counts.
halo.offline_body: At 795 MB, the Q8_0 model runs completely offline on an iPhone 16 Pro Max via llama.cpp Metal at roughly 505 ms per decision step.

lab.title: How a 0.8B model beats frontier APIs in real time
lab.lead: Click any architecture node or switch junctions below to inspect the live engine data structures, `/v1/systemone` prompts, 5-second teacher rollouts, and ablation results.

ui.diagram_hint: Click any pipeline stage (01-04) to inspect its contract and source code

ch1.title: How `/v1/systemone` turns chat generation into 1-token scoring
ch1.question: How much decode work does single-token scoring remove from a short JSON response?

n1.title: Junction Discovery
n1.body: The 30 Hz game loop never pauses for the model. Instead, it scans ahead along Pac-Man's current corridor to find the next tile with 2 or more legal exits.

n2.title: Option Letter Mapping
n2.body: Legal directions (`up`, `left`, `down`, `right`, `back`) are mapped to single uppercase option letters (`A`, `B`, `C`, `D`) inside Ollama's `/v1/systemone` schema.
n2.io_out: Chat-templated prompt ending at answer token

n3.title: 1-Token Logit Scoring
n3.body: Instead of decoding a 7-token JSON object (`{"move":"left"}`), the server runs one prefill forward pass, masks logits to valid option letters, and returns softmax probabilities.

n4.title: Non-Blocking Turn Queue
n4.body: When the HTTP response returns, the agent loop verifies that Pac-Man has not yet passed the junction tile and queues the turn for exact execution at the tile center.

ch1.latency_note: Component estimate: {prefill} ms prefill plus {decode} ms per additional token. M3 Ultra and RTX 5090 use recorded 0.8B component timings. H100 uses illustrative assumptions. These totals exclude end-to-end request overhead.
ch1.wb_probs_title: Local rollout weights, not model probabilities
ch1.prompt_toggle: Preview the /v1/systemone prompt; no Ollama request is sent
ch1.takeaway: Constrained single-token logit scoring removes JSON syntax errors and saves 6 autoregressive decode steps on every junction.

ch2.title: Why compact BFS features beat ASCII maps under a 30 Hz clock
ch2.question: Why do 0.8B to 4B models fail on ASCII grids (confidence 0.02 to 0.14) but succeed on BFS features (0.60 to 0.90)?

n1.title: Exact Maze BFS
n1.body: For each legal exit at the upcoming junction, the engine runs a breadth-first search over walkable tiles to compute exact step counts around corners and through tunnels.

n2.title: Fact-Only Feature JSON
n2.body: The encoder reports pure geometric facts per exit (`ghost`, `ghost_coming`, `pellets`, `food`, `power`) without rules or verdicts, in ~260 tokens vs ~630 for `ascii-full`.

n3.title: Realtime Travel Budget
n3.body: At level 1, Pac-Man moves at 7.58 tiles per second. A 55 ms local call costs 0.42 tiles of travel; a 220 ms slow call costs 1.67 tiles and risks missing close junctions.

n4.title: Lookahead Pipelining
n4.body: When Pac-Man is within `lookahead` tiles of a junction whose turn is already planned, the loop queries the model for the junction after it so decisions arrive before arrival.

ch2.wb_encoder_title: Compare State Encoders at This Junction
ch2.wb_horizon_title: Realtime Latency vs Junction Arrival Budget
ch2.horizon_fresh_body: Pac-Man travels {traveled} tiles during the call and reaches the junction ({dist} tiles away) with {margin} tiles to spare.
ch2.horizon_stale_body: Pac-Man travels {traveled} tiles during the call, passing the junction ({dist} tiles away) by {margin} tiles before the answer arrives.
ch2.takeaway: Small models should not waste capacity parsing 2D ASCII coordinates. Pre-computing exact maze distances in code raises model confidence from <0.14 to >0.60 and halves prefill tokens.

ch3.title: How 5-second teacher lookahead distills into a zero-lookahead 0.8B student
ch3.question: How can `pacman-0.8b-qwen` score 425 pellets using only `features` when off-the-shelf models cap out at 237?

n1.title: 5-Second Engine Rollouts
n1.body: At labeling time only, the engine clones the state for each legal option and simulates 5 seconds (150 ticks) of greedy play against real ghost AI to observe survival and points.

n2.title: 27B Teacher Labeling
n2.body: Qwen3.5-27B receives both the immediate `features` and the 5-second `peek()` outcomes across 54,193 junction states, choosing moves that avoid multi-junction ghost pincers.

n3.title: Information-Gap SFT
n3.body: The 0.8B student (`Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base`) is trained with LoRA (`r=32, alpha=64`) on `features` alone, learning to infer future danger and reward from current-state cues.

n4.title: Quantized Edge Runtime
n4.body: Exported to Q8_0 GGUF, the distilled 0.8B model scores 425 pellets in real time (6.2x base `tev1:0.8b`) while running in 55 ms on desktop or ~505 ms offline on iPhone.

ch3.moves_summary: Immediate greedy rule picks '{student}' · Teacher lookahead picks '{teacher}'
ch3.col_teacher: What 27B Teacher Saw at Labeling ({sec}s peek)
ch3.takeaway: Lookahead belongs in the training pipeline, not at inference. Giving the teacher 5-second rollouts lets a 0.8B student internalize multi-junction foresight with zero runtime search cost.

ch4.title: What mattered, what was statistical noise, and what broke along the way
ch4.question: Did soft KL targets, BF16 H100 teachers, or a 671B MoE teacher beat the 32-minute RTX 5090 baseline?

n1.title: vLLM Logprob Mask Bug
n1.body: In vLLM, `guided_choice` masks logits during sampling, but default `raw_logprobs` computes top-k BEFORE the mask. Out-of-option tokens (`D`, `\n`) pushed valid options out of top-20 in 86.4% of rows until `--logprobs-mode processed_logprobs` was set.

n2.title: Soft KL vs Hard CE
n2.body: Even with exact processed logprobs, the 27B open-source teacher had a mean top-1 probability of 0.996 (exceeding 0.99 on 97.6% of states). Soft KL distillation (409) matched hard labels (425).

n3.title: 6-Run Ablation Equivalence
n3.body: Across NVFP4 vs BF16, 27B vs 671B MoE open-source teachers, hard vs soft targets, and CUDA vs MLX, all 6 distilled 0.8B students landed within 10-game noise (SE ~30 pellets).

n4.title: The Specialization Trade-Off
n4.body: Fine-tuning `tev1:0.8b` exclusively on Pac-Man junctions multiplied game performance by 6.2x (69 -> 425) while reducing accuracy on 194 general decision questions from 0.66 to 0.53.

ch4.mask_explain: Suppose valid options are A, B, C, and raw token probabilities are A=49%, C=14%, D=12%, B=11%. Inspect what top-3 truncation retains:
ch4.dropped_warning: Bug triggered: out-of-option token 'D' pushed valid option '{dropped}' out of top-3!
ch4.retained_ok: Mask applied before top-k: all valid options ({retained}) are preserved.
ch4.takeaway: Once the representation (`features`) and teacher lookahead (`peek5s`) are right, a 32-minute single-GPU LoRA run captures the full gain. Switching teachers, precision, or soft targets stays within noise.

ch5.kicker: Chapter 05 · Production Bare-Metal Infrastructure Case Study
ch5.title: Transferring the Exact Same Pipeline to OpenShift Bare-Metal RCA
ch5.question: What happens when we take the unchanged `decision-pacman` distillation + `/v1/systemone` pipeline and apply it to 23-class OpenShift IPI / Metal3 / Ironic provisioning failure root-cause analysis (`baremetal-rca`)?

n1.title: 23-Class RCA Schema
n1.body: Each OpenShift / Metal3 failure is encoded as compact JSON (`bmo_phase`, `provisioning_state`, `hardware_vendor`, `boot_mode`, `network_stack`, `symptom_primary`, `log_excerpt`) and scored across 23 lettered failure categories (`A..W`).
n1.io_in: BMH / Ironic / Installer logs & CR status

n2.title: 1-H100 LoRA Training
n2.body: Unchanged `training/build_sft.py` and `training/train.py` fine-tune `tev1-0.8b` on 1,128 27B teacher rows. Holdout validation accuracy jumps from 21.8% (zero-shot) to 90.2% in 3 minutes on 1 H100.

n3.title: Synthetic Textbook Eval
n3.body: On 333 held-out synthetic bare-metal incidents (seeds 1000-1002), the 76 ms `rca-0.8b` student reaches 94.0% top-1 accuracy (98.5% top-3), beating the 671B MoE open-source model zero-shot (81.7%) and the 27B open-source model (65.2%).

n4.title: 48 Real GitHub Issues Audit
n4.body: On 48 real OpenShift, Metal3, and Ironic issues, the student scores 22.9% and DeepSeek scores 41.7%. Real cases contain 70.8% product bugs, unlike the approximately balanced training set. This class shift, incomplete reports, and label ambiguity are possible causes; no ablation has isolated their effects.

cases.synth_1000_diag: In-distribution win (94.0% synthetic split). Clear HTTP 401 Redfish traceback on Cisco UCS. `rca-0.8b` assigns 89.1% probability to `bmc_credentials` in 76 ms, matching the 671B MoE open-source model at half the latency.
cases.bmo_1098_diag: Real config issue where the 0.8B student beats the comment-biased teacher. The operator passed an `http://` BMC URL while Metal3 defaulted to HTTPS (`tls: recordHeaderError`). Both `rca-0.8b` (61.6%) and the zero-shot 671B MoE model pick `bmc_driver_mismatch`, whereas the teacher with comments got distracted by maintainer discussion and mislabeled it `product_bug`.
cases.installer_10108_diag: A real product bug missed by the student. An openshift/installer defect dropped loadBalancer: UserManaged while generating AgentClusterInstall. The student instead chose api_ingress_vip_dns with 86.9% probability; DeepSeek chose product_bug. The example alone does not establish whether class balance caused the error.
cases.ironic_137_diag: Condition #3 failure (No oracle for reporter prose). The reporter omitted `boot_mode: uefi` on `redfish-virtualmedia`, causing legacy BIOS ISO build to fail on missing `isolinux.bin`, and wrongly blamed the container packaging in the issue body. Without a simulator rollout to test the config, both `rca-0.8b` (80.2%) and the zero-shot 671B MoE model fall for the reporter's `product_bug` theory.

ch5.takeaway: The student learns synthetic cases well, but its real-case score remains 22.9%. Test better incident inputs, representative training examples, and independently reviewed labels before concluding that this approach is ready for deployment.

paths.title: Need more than an off-the-shelf model? Two paths
paths.lead: A plain open model gets you to Jev's level. To go beyond it, there are two paths, each with its own cost.
paths.a_body: Fine-tuning is no silver bullet, but it lets you make deliberate trade-offs across size, speed, cost, domain, and intelligence.
paths.b_body: Switch to a bigger model and let it think. When the game waits for it, a 27B model goes from {off} to {on} pellets, at about 2.4 seconds per move.

recipe.note: That is the trade-off: on 194 general decision questions unrelated to Pac-Man, it fell from 0.66 to 0.53. It was built for this one task.

builder.title: From user to builder
builder.closed_body: You use them when they work. When they fail, your only choice is switching providers.
builder.yours_body: Size, speed, cost, domain, and intelligence: you can adjust every single parameter yourself.
builder.quote: Being able to build and choosing not to is very different from having no other choice.

takeaways.title: Three prerequisites for self-trained small models
takeaways.lead: Comparing a simulator benchmark (`decision-pacman`) against production infrastructure tickets (`baremetal-rca`) proves that three prerequisites must hold simultaneously.
takeaways.t1_title: Closed choices & strict latency, where off-the-shelf Jev is not enough
takeaways.t1_body: The historical Pac-Man results are 69 pellets for tev1:0.8b, 178 for Jev, and 425 for the distilled student. RCA is also a closed choice, but its 21.8% pretraining figure measures validation accuracy on a different split.
takeaways.t2_title: A real-case test exposes what synthetic accuracy misses
takeaways.t2_body: Pac-Man uses engine facts and teacher labels informed by rollouts. RCA uses generated training summaries and real issue reports for evaluation. Its student scores 94.0% on synthetic cases and 22.9% on real issues. Incomplete reports, class imbalance, and ambiguous labels are possible explanations; this experiment does not isolate their effects.
takeaways.t3_title: Disciplined training to prevent synthetic prior & multi-epoch overfitting
takeaways.t3_body: RCA reaches 90.2% validation accuracy and 94.0% synthetic accuracy, but 22.9% on real issues. A mismatch between training and deployment data is a hypothesis to test. In Pac-Man, training two epochs instead of one raised offline validation accuracy but lowered game score from 423 to 266.

cta.title: Ready to move from user to builder?
cta.body: The course walks you through the entire pipeline on your own task: pick a task, select a teacher, label data, train, and deploy to mobile.

footer.run_title: Run it on your own machine
footer.fineprint: RCA uses 333 synthetic cases and 48 real OpenShift/Metal3/Ironic issues. Historical student results use an H100. Pac-Man uses seeds 100–109, with historical averages over 10, 20, or 30 games. The dated comparison identifies the fresh OpenAI and Jev runs.

evaluation.title: Decision APIs and ordinary LLMs on the same tasks
evaluation.lead: Fresh tests compare GPT-6 Luna through Decisions and Responses, GPT-6.1 Terra through Responses, and Jev 1.13.0 and 1.14.0. The fine-tuned model results remain labeled as historical measurements.
evaluation.cost_pending: Evaluation in progress; cost is incomplete.
evaluation.cost_incomplete: {requests} requests; {unknown} have unresolved usage. This is a lower bound.
evaluation.cost_basis: Calculated from response token usage at published list prices. This is an estimate, not an invoice. Only this session is included.
evaluation.pacman_protocol: Current-state features, realtime clock, 1× speed, seeds 100–109, 300-second cap. Pellets are averaged per game. Latency is the mean of per-game p50 values.
evaluation.historical_note: All fresh tests use the same Linux client and task protocol. The Decisions run came first, then the two Jev versions ran together, followed by the two Responses models together. Network and provider load can differ between batches. Historical local runs used an M3 Ultra; hosted runs used its network path. These rows do not establish a simultaneous paired ranking or a compute-speed comparison. Historical averages include 10, 20, or 30 games.
evaluation.rca_title: RCA on the same held-out cases
evaluation.rca_protocol: One of 23 root causes, selected from facts and option descriptions. The label is withheld from the model. Synthetic cases: {synthetic}. Real issues: {real}. Failures count as incorrect.
evaluation.majority_note: Always choosing product_bug scores {accuracy} on the real set. Compare every model with this majority-class baseline.
evaluation.rca_limits: Real labels come from one annotator, and most cases are product bugs. This small, skewed set cannot establish reliable per-class rankings. The inputs were already summarized. These costs cover classification only; preparation and subsequent investigation are excluded.
evaluation.rca_source: Recorded RCA baselines and dataset method
evaluation.rca_bar_note: OpenAI and both Jev versions are measured on {date}; student and DeepSeek rows are historical. All rows use the same evaluation cases. Latencies come from different serving environments.
evaluation.formula: OpenAI cost is the sum of uncached input, cached reads, cache writes, and output tokens, each multiplied by its route's rate above and divided by 1,000,000. Cached reads and writes are subsets of input. Reasoning tokens are a subset of output and are charged only once.
evaluation.usage_note: Jev does not report cache counts, shown as N/A. Reasoning is N/A where the API does not report it. OpenAI cache-write rates shown here use the default 30-minute retention. Connectivity checks are included. Historical model costs, local compute, RCA preparation, and downstream LLM work are excluded. Pac-Man runs can issue different numbers of requests because latency and survival differ; a lower game bill does not imply cheaper equal-work inference. RCA uses a fixed number of cases.
evaluation.jev_formula: Jev USD = input × 0.042 / 1,000,000. Output is free for both tested Jev versions.
evaluation.responses_protocol: GPT-6.1 Luna was unavailable in the account model list, so this run uses GPT-6 Luna. Both Responses models use reasoning effort none, the standard service tier, and strict JSON with one legal choice. This measures a low-cost configuration, not each model's best possible quality.
evaluation.pacman_cost_scope: Cost is the API total for the games in each row, excluding connectivity checks. Historical costs were not recorded.
evaluation.rca_cost_scope: Cost combines all {synthetic} synthetic and {real} real-case classification calls, excluding connectivity checks. Historical costs were not recorded.

workflow.title: Classification is one part of the RCA bill
workflow.lead: In this workflow, a decision model selects a root-cause category. LLMs still prepare evidence, investigate the incident, and explain what to do. Savings depend on how much of the original bill that single step accounts for.

evidence.title: Collect evidence
evidence.body: Logs, metrics, incident history, and system state.

prepare.title: Prepare the input
prepare.body: Triage, summarize, or structure evidence for the classifier. Extra calls add cost.

classify.title: Choose a category
classify.body: Select one of the 23 root-cause options from prepared facts.

investigate.title: Analyze the cause
investigate.body: Test hypotheses, connect evidence, and explain why the failure happened.

resolve.title: Resolve and verify
resolve.body: Propose a fix, check the outcome, and write the incident report.

workflow.evidence_path: Original evidence may still need to reach the downstream LLM. A category or summary does not replace the logs needed for investigation.
workflow.diagram_note: This is a proposed workflow, not an end-to-end benchmark. Stage widths do not represent cost. The tests above classify inputs that were already summarized.
workflow.calculator_title: How much can the full workflow save?
workflow.calculator_lead: Change the share spent on classification, its replacement cost, and any additional LLM preparation. All other work stays the same in this example.

classificationShare.label: Classification share of the original bill
classificationShare.hint: f · Percentage of the entire baseline cost.

replacementPercent.label: New classifier cost relative to the old step
replacementPercent.hint: r · 10% means this step becomes 90% cheaper.

extraPreparation.label: Extra LLM preparation cost
extraPreparation.hint: h · Percentage of the entire baseline cost, added on top.

workflow.limit: If other work stays fixed, even a free classifier can save at most the original classification share. Added preparation reduces that saving. A classifier that enables early exits or fewer later LLM calls changes this assumption.
workflow.accounting: Count only preparation added by the new design. Shared preprocessing is already part of the baseline. These sliders are hypothetical cost ratios, not token-price ratios or measured pipeline savings.
workflow.scope_title: What the measured cost leaves out
workflow.scope_body: The RCA comparison measures a choice among fixed categories. Its inputs already contain prepared facts. The reported API costs exclude generating those summaries, gathering more evidence, explaining the cause, and validating a fix. Those steps can still require LLM calls.
workflow.context_body: A deployment's context budget and input schema can require selection, chunking, or LLM summaries. That adds processing cost and may drop evidence the later analysis needs. A short context window is not a universal property of decision models.
workflow.context_limits: Jev 1.13 and 1.14 document defaults of 64k tokens per request and 32k per question. An opt-in mode allows 262k for both, with vendor warnings about speed and accuracy. The tested runs use the defaults.
